questions.subtopic: Linux 64-Bit (elf64) & 32-Bit (elf_i386) Build Commands
questions.concept: Assembling, Linking, and Running 64-bit vs. 32-bit NASM Programs on Linux (Slides 6.26–6.27)
questions.question: According to Slides 6.26 and 6.27 (`ch06_hopngu_phan1.pdf`), what are the exact terminal commands used on Linux to assemble and link a **64-bit** NASM program (`first.asm`) versus a **32-bit** NASM program (`first32.asm`) into an executable `./a.out`?
options: 64-bit: `nasm -f elf64 first.asm` then `ld first.o`; 32-bit (diagram on Slide 6.27): `nasm -f elf first32.asm` then `ld -m elf_i386 first32.o`
NASM executables run directly without linking via `ld`
questions.explanationEn: Slide 6.26 shows the 64-bit workflow: `nasm -f elf64 first.asm` -> `ld first.o` -> `./a.out`. Slide 6.27 shows the 32-bit workflow: `nasm -f elf first32.asm` (note the slide bullet text has a typo saying `elf64` while the terminal screenshot shows `nasm -f elf first32.asm`) followed by `ld -m elf_i386 first32.o` -> `./a.out`.
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 6.26–6.27: Quy trình dịch và liên kết 64-bit trên Linux là `nasm -f elf64 first.asm` và `ld first.o`. Với 32-bit là `nasm -f elf first32.asm` và `ld -m elf_i386 first32.o`, sau đó chạy `./a.out`.

questions.subtopic: NASM Sections (.data, .bss, .text) & Statement Types
questions.concept: NASM Program Sections (.data, .bss, .text) and Statement Types (Slides 6.28–6.30)
questions.question: In a NASM assembly program (Slides 6.28–6.30), what is the purpose of each of the three sections (`section .data`, `section .bss`, `section .text`), and what are the three types of assembly language statements?
options: `section .data` holds executable code; `section .bss` holds constants; `section .text` holds uninitialized arrays
All variables and instructions must be placed inside `section .bss`

`section .data` declares initialized data/constants; `section .bss` declares uninitialized variables (reserved memory); `section .text` holds the executable code (starting with `global _start` or `global main`); the three statement types are (1) Executable instructions, (2) Assembler directives (pseudo-ops), and (3) Macros
Macros are executed directly by the ALU without assembler translation
questions.explanationEn: Slides 6.28–6.29 explain that `.data` is for declaring initialized data or constants, `.bss` is for declaring uninitialized variables, and `.text` is for keeping the actual executable code. Slide 6.30 lists the three statement types: Executable instructions, Assembler directives (pseudo-ops), and Macros (text substitution).
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 6.28–6.30: `section .data` dùng khai báo dữ liệu/hằng số đã khởi tạo; `section .bss` khai báo biến chưa khởi tạo; `section .text` chứa mã lệnh thực thi. Ba loại câu lệnh trong hợp ngữ là: Lệnh thực thi (Executable instructions), Chỉ thị biên dịch (Assembler directives / pseudo-ops), và Macro.

questions.subtopic: Register, Immediate & Direct Addressing Modes
questions.concept: Identifying Register, Immediate, and Direct Addressing Modes (Slides 6.32–6.34)
questions.question:
Examine the three instructions illustrated in the diagrams on Slides 6.32, 6.33, and 6.34 (`ch06_hopngu_phan1.pdf`):
1) `movq %rax, %rdx`
2) `movw $5, %dx`
3) `movb 0x20a, %dl`
What are the addressing modes of the source operands in instructions (1), (2), and (3), and what is the final value of `%rdx` in (3) if ` initially %rdx = 0xffffffffffffffff` and `Mem[0x20a] = 0x55` (inside `0xcc55aa33` at `0x00208`)?
options: (1) Immediate mode, (2) Direct mode, (3) Register mode; `%rdx` becomes `0x000000000000020a`
(1) Direct mode, (2) Register mode, (3) Immediate mode; `%rdx` becomes `0xffffffffffffffcc`
(1) Register mode (`%rax`), (2) Immediate mode (`$5`), (3) Direct addressing mode (`0x20a`); in (3), `%dl` is loaded with byte `0x55`, so `%rdx` becomes `0xffffffffffffff55`
All three instructions use Indirect Scaled-Index addressing
questions.explanationEn: Slide 6.32 shows `movq %rax, %rdx` where both operands use Register Mode. Slide 6.33 shows `movw $5, %dx` where source `$5` uses Immediate Mode (`%rdx` becomes `0xffffffffffff0005`). Slide 6.34 shows `movb 0x20a, %dl` where source `0x20a` uses Direct Addressing Mode, loading byte `0x55` into the lowest 8 bits `%dl` so `%rdx` becomes `0xffffffffffffff55`.
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 6.32–6.34: (1) `movq %rax, %rdx` dùng chế độ Thanh ghi (Register mode); (2) `movw $5, %dx` có toán hạng nguồn `$5` dùng chế độ Tức thời (Immediate mode); (3) `movb 0x20a, %dl` có toán hạng nguồn `0x20a` dùng chế độ Địa chỉ trực tiếp (Direct Addressing mode), nạp byte `55h` vào `%dl` làm `%rdx = 0xffffffffffffff55`.

questions.subtopic: Initialized Data Directives (db, dw, dd, dq, dt)
questions.concept: NASM Data Directives (db, dw, dd, dq, dt, times, resw, resb) Sizes & Values (Slides 6.40–6.46)
questions.question: Based on Slides 6.40–6.46 (`ch06_hopngu_phan1.pdf`), what are the exact byte sizes of the NASM directives `db`, `dw`, `dd`, `dq`, and `dt`, what is the decimal value initialized by `L5 db 17o` (Slide 6.43), and how many total bytes are allocated by `L10 db "word", 0`, `L11 times 100 db 0`, and `L20 resw 100`?
options: Sizes: `db` = 1B, `dw` = 4B, `dd` = 8B, `dq` = 16B, `dt` = 32B; `L5 db 17o` initializes 17 decimal; `L20 resw 100` reserves 100 bytes

Sizes: `db` = 1B, `dw` = 2B, `dd` = 4B, `dq` = 8B, `dt` = 10B (80-bit float); `L5 db 17o` initializes 1 byte to `15` decimal (`1×8 + 7`); `L10 db "word", 0` allocates 5 bytes; `L11 times 100 db 0` allocates 100 bytes; `L20 resw 100` reserves 200 uninitialized bytes (100 × 2-byte words)
questions.explanationEn: Slide 6.41 lists unit sizes: byte (`B` = 1B), word (`W` = 2B), double word (`D` = 4B), quad word (`Q` = 8B), ten bytes (`T` = 10B = 80-bit float). Slide 6.43 shows `L5 db 17o` initializes 1 byte to `17_8 = 1×8 + 7 = 15` in decimal. Slide 6.44 shows `L10 db "word", 0` defines a 5-byte null-terminated string (`'w','o','r','d',0`). Slide 6.45 shows `times 100 db 0` allocates 100 bytes. Slide 6.46 shows `L20 resw 100` reserves 100 uninitialized 2-byte words = 200 bytes.
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 6.41–6.46: Kích thước các chỉ thị là `db` = 1B, `dw` = 2B, `dd` = 4B, `dq` = 8B, `dt` = 10B. Chỉ thị `L5 db 17o` khởi tạo 1 byte có giá trị hệ bát phân `17_8 = 1×8 + 7 = 15` thập phân. `L10 db "word", 0` cấp phát 5 bytes (4 ký tự + 1 byte null `0`). `L11 times 100 db 0` cấp phát 100 bytes. `L20 resw 100` dành riêng 100 từ 2-byte = 200 bytes chưa khởi tạo.

questions.subtopic: MOV, MOVZX, MOVSX, XCHG, LEA, PUSH & POP
questions.concept: Tracing MOVZX vs. MOVSX and LEA vs. PUSH/POP (Slides 22–23 of ch06_part1_2.pdf)
questions.question:
Trace the two assembly fragments on Slides 22 and 23 of `ch06_part1_2.pdf`:
Fragment A:
```nasm
section .data
  num db 0FFh
section .text
  mov al, [num]
  movzx ebx, al
  movsx ecx, al
```
Fragment B:
```nasm
  mov rax, 100
  push rax
  mov rax, 200
  pop rbx
```
What are the final values of `AL`, `EBX`, `ECX` in Fragment A, and `RAX`, `RBX` in Fragment B?
options: Fragment A: `AL = FFh`, `EBX = FFFFFFFFh`, `ECX = 000000FFh`; Fragment B: `RAX = 100`, `RBX = 200`
Fragment A: `AL = FFh`, `EBX = 000000FFh` (zero-extended), `ECX = FFFFFFFFh` (sign-extended); Fragment B: `RAX = 200`, `RBX = 100`
questions.explanationEn: Slide 22 shows that `num db 0FFh` loaded into `AL` gives `AL = FFh` (MSB bit 7 = 1). `movzx ebx, al` zero-extends `AL` into 32-bit `EBX = 000000FFh`. `movsx ecx, al` sign-extends `AL` (replicating sign bit 1) into 32-bit `ECX = FFFFFFFFh`. Slide 23 shows `push rax` pushes `100` onto the stack, `mov rax, 200` changes `RAX` to `200`, and `pop rbx` pops `100` from the top of the stack into `RBX = 100`.
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 22–23 (`ch06_part1_2.pdf`): Trong Đoạn A, `AL = FFh` (có bit dấu bằng 1); lệnh `movzx ebx, al` mở rộng không dấu thành `EBX = 000000FFh`; lệnh `movsx ecx, al` mở rộng có dấu thành `ECX = FFFFFFFFh`. Trong Đoạn B, `push rax` đẩy 100 vào stack, sau đó `RAX` đổi thành 200, rồi `pop rbx` lấy giá trị 100 từ đỉnh stack ra `RBX = 100`.

questions.subtopic: ADD, ADC, SUB, SBB, INC, DEC, NEG & CMP
questions.concept: Tracing Arithmetic Sequence (ADD, SUB, INC, DEC, NEG) (Slide 25 of ch06_part1_2.pdf)
questions.question:
Trace the arithmetic instruction sequence on Slide 25 (`ch06_part1_2.pdf`):
```nasm
mov eax, 20
mov ebx, 8
add eax, ebx
sub eax, 5
inc eax
dec ebx
neg ebx
```
What are the final decimal and 32-bit hexadecimal values of `EAX` and `EBX`?
questions.explanationEn: Tracing Slide 25 step-by-step: (1) `mov eax, 20` -> EAX=20; (2) `mov ebx, 8` -> EBX=8; (3) `add eax, ebx` -> EAX=20+8=28; (4) `sub eax, 5` -> EAX=28-5=23; (5) `inc eax` -> EAX=23+1=24 (`0x18`); (6) `dec ebx` -> EBX=8-1=7; (7) `neg ebx` (two's complement negation) -> EBX=-7 (`0xFFFFFFF9`).
questions.explanationVi: Theo bảng vết thực thi trên Slide 25 (`ch06_part1_2.pdf`): `EAX` lần lượt nhận giá trị: `20 -> (+8) = 28 -> (-5) = 23 -> (+1) = 24 (0x18)`. `EBX` lần lượt nhận giá trị: `8 -> (-1) = 7 -> (đổi dấu bù 2 bằng NEG) = -7 (0xFFFFFFF9)`.
questions.formula: NEG dest => dest = 0 - dest (Two's complement negation)

questions.subtopic: Evaluating CF, ZF, SF, OF on 8-Bit Arithmetic & CMP
questions.concept: Evaluating AL and Status Flags (CF, ZF, SF, OF) on 8-Bit ADD and SUB (Slide 29 of ch06_part1_2.pdf)
questions.question:
Compare the three 8-bit flag examples on Slide 29 (`ch06_part1_2.pdf` and Slides 6.52–6.53 of `ch06_hopngu_phan1.pdf`):
Case 1: `mov al, 255` followed by `add al, 1`
Case 2: `mov al, 127` followed by `add al, 1`
Case 3: `mov al, 5` followed by `sub al, 8`
What are the resulting values of `(AL, CF, ZF, SF, OF)` for each of the three cases?
options: Case 1: `(AL=00h, CF=1, ZF=1, SF=0, OF=0)`; Case 2: `(AL=80h, CF=0, ZF=0, SF=1, OF=1)`; Case 3: `(AL=FDh, CF=1, ZF=0, SF=1, OF=0)`
Case 1: `(AL=FFh, CF=0, ZF=0, SF=1, OF=1)`; Case 2: `(AL=80h, CF=1, ZF=1, SF=0, OF=0)`; Case 3: `(AL=03h, CF=0, ZF=0, SF=0, OF=1)`
Case 1: `(AL=00h, CF=1, ZF=1, SF=0, OF=1)`; Case 2: `(AL=80h, CF=1, ZF=0, SF=1, OF=0)`; Case 3: `(AL=FDh, CF=0, ZF=0, SF=1, OF=1)`
questions.explanationEn: Slide 29 shows all three tables: Case 1 (`255 + 1`, i.e., `FFh + 1 = 100h`): 8-bit `AL = 00h`, unsigned carry out sets `CF = 1`, zero result sets `ZF = 1`, MSB is 0 (`SF = 0`), and signed `-1 + 1 = 0` has no signed overflow (`OF = 0`). Case 2 (`127 + 1`, i.e., `7Fh + 1 = 80h`): `AL = 80h` (-128 signed), no unsigned carry (`CF = 0`), non-zero (`ZF = 0`), MSB is 1 (`SF = 1`), and adding two positive signed numbers (`+127 + 1`) produced a negative result (`-128`), so signed overflow `OF = 1`! Case 3 (`5 - 8 = -3 = FDh`): `AL = FDh`, unsigned borrow sets `CF = 1`, non-zero (`ZF = 0`), MSB is 1 (`SF = 1`), and signed `5 - 8 = -3` fits in `[-128, +127]`, so `OF = 0`.
questions.explanationVi: Theo 3 bảng trên Slide 29 (`ch06_part1_2.pdf`): TH1 (`255 + 1 = FFh + 1`): `AL = 00h`, tràn không dấu `CF = 1`, bằng 0 nên `ZF = 1`, `SF = 0`, theo số có dấu là `-1 + 1 = 0` không tràn nên `OF = 0`. TH2 (`127 + 1 = 7Fh + 1`): `AL = 80h`, không tràn không dấu `CF = 0`, `ZF = 0`, bit dấu bằng 1 (`SF = 1`), tràn số có dấu (`+127 + 1 = -128`) nên `OF = 1`. TH3 (`5 - 8 = -3`): `AL = FDh`, có mượn không dấu `CF = 1`, `ZF = 0`, âm nên `SF = 1`, không tràn có dấu nên `OF = 0`.
questions.formula: CF = Unsigned Carry/Borrow; OF = Signed Two's Complement Overflow

questions.subtopic: Unconditional & Conditional Jumps (JMP, JE/JZ, JG/JL, JA/JB)
questions.concept: Tracing CMP and Conditional Jump JL (Slides 30 & 33 of ch06_part1_2.pdf)
questions.question:
Trace the conditional jump program on Slide 33 (`ch06_part1_2.pdf`):
```nasm
  mov eax, 10   ; int a = 10
  mov ebx, 20   ; int b = 20
  cmp eax, ebx  ; compares a and b by computing eax - ebx (10 - 20 = -10)
  jl less
  mov ecx, eax
  jmp finish
less:
  mov ecx, ebx
finish:
```
How does `cmp eax, ebx` affect `EAX` and the status flags (`CF, SF, OF, ZF`), is the `jl less` branch taken, and what is the final value of `ECX`?
options: `cmp` subtracts `20` from `10` without modifying `EAX` (`EAX` remains `10`), setting `CF = 1, SF = 1, OF = 0, ZF = 0` (note Slide 30 shows `CF=1, SF=1, OF=0, ZF=0` for `15 - 20`); since `SF != OF` (`10 < 20`), `jl less` IS taken and `ECX = 20`
`cmp` overwrites `EAX` with `-10`, `jl less` is not taken, and `ECX = 10`
questions.explanationEn: Slides 30 and 33 explain that `CMP` subtracts its second operand from its first operand (`10 - 20 = -10`) and updates the status flags without storing the subtraction result (`EAX = 10, EBX = 20`). Because `10 < 20` (signed less than: `SF = 1, OF = 0`), `jl less` branches to `less:`, executing `mov ecx, ebx` so `ECX = 20`.
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 30 và 33: Lệnh `cmp eax, ebx` thực hiện phép trừ ngầm `eax - ebx` (`10 - 20 = -10`) để cập nhật cờ trạng thái (`SF = 1, OF = 0, ZF = 0`) mà không làm thay đổi giá trị `EAX = 10`. Vì `10 < 20` nên lệnh nhảy có điều kiện `jl less` được thực hiện, gán `ECX = EBX = 20`.

questions.subtopic: Procedure Calls (CALL, RET, INT, IRET)
questions.concept: Tracing CALL, RET, and LOOP Instructions (Slides 38–39 of ch06_part1_2.pdf)
questions.question:
Trace the two code fragments on Slides 38 (`PROCEDURE CALLS`) and 39 (`LOOP INSTRUCTIONS`) of `ch06_part1_2.pdf`:
Fragment 1:
```nasm
  mov rax, 5
  call double_value
  jmp done
double_value:
  add rax, rax
  ret
done:
```
Fragment 2:
```nasm
  mov rcx, 5
  mov rax, 0
sum_loop:
  add rax, rcx
  loop sum_loop
```
What mechanism do `CALL` and `RET` use, and what are the final values of `RAX` in Fragment 1 and `RAX`, `RCX` in Fragment 2?
options: `CALL` pushes the return address onto the stack and jumps to `double_value`, while `RET` pops the return address from the stack to resume execution, leaving `RAX = 10` in Fragment 1; in Fragment 2, `LOOP` decrements `RCX` each iteration and jumps to `sum_loop` while `RCX != 0`, computing `5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15`, leaving `RAX = 15` and `RCX = 0`
`CALL` stores the return address in `RCX`, causing an infinite loop
questions.explanationEn: Slide 38 shows `CALL` pushes the return address onto the stack and transfers execution to `double_value` (`add rax, rax` -> `5 + 5 = 10`), and `RET` retrieves the return address from the stack and resumes at `jmp done`. Slide 39 shows `LOOP` decrements `RCX` and jumps if `RCX != 0`, summing `5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15` into `RAX` and ending with `RCX = 0`.
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 38–39: Lệnh `CALL` đẩy địa chỉ trả về vào stack và nhảy tới thủ tục `double_value` (`RAX = 5 + 5 = 10`), sau đó `RET` lấy địa chỉ trả về từ stack để quay lại. Ở Đoạn 2, lệnh `LOOP` tự động giảm bộ đếm `RCX` đi 1 sau mỗi vòng và nhảy về `sum_loop` nếu `RCX != 0`, tính tổng `5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15` vào `RAX` và kết thúc khi `RCX = 0`.

questions.subtopic: Unsigned Multiplication (MUL 8/16/32-bit into AX, DX:AX, EDX:EAX)
questions.concept: Tracing 8-Bit, 16-Bit, and 32-Bit Unsigned MUL (Slides 45–47 of ch06_part1_2.pdf)
questions.question:
Verify the three unsigned `MUL` examples on Slides 45, 46, and 47 of `ch06_part1_2.pdf`:
1) 8-bit: `mov al, 20` / `mov bl, 15` / `mul bl` (`20 × 15 = 300 = 012Ch`)
2) 16-bit: `mov ax, 300` / `mov bx, 400` / `mul bx` (`300 × 400 = 120,000 = 0001D4C0h`)
3) 32-bit: `mov eax, 100000` / `mov ebx, 70000` / `mul ebx` (`7,000,000,000 = 00000001A13B8600h`)
Where are the products stored and what are the exact register values after each `mul`?
options: 1) Stored in `AL = 2Ch` (`AH` unchanged); 2) Stored in `AX = D4C0h` (`DX` unchanged); 3) Stored in `EAX = A13B8600h` (`EDX` unchanged)
1) Stored in `AX = 012Ch` (`AH = 01h, AL = 2Ch`); 2) Stored in `DX:AX` with `DX = 0001h` and `AX = D4C0h`; 3) Stored in `EDX:EAX` with `EDX = 00000001h` and `EAX = A13B8600h`
All three products are stored in `EBX`
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 45–47 (`ch06_part1_2.pdf`): (1) Nhân 8-bit `AL × BL -> AX = 012Ch` (`AH = 01h, AL = 2Ch`). (2) Nhân 16-bit `AX × BX -> DX:AX = 0001D4C0h` (`DX = 0001h, AX = D4C0h`). (3) Nhân 32-bit `EAX × EBX -> EDX:EAX = 00000001A13B8600h` (`EDX = 00000001h, EAX = A13B8600h`).
questions.formula: 8b: AX = AL*src; 16b: DX:AX = AX*src; 32b: EDX:EAX = EAX*src

questions.subtopic: Signed Multiplication (IMUL 1, 2, and 3-Operand Forms)
questions.concept: Tracing 1-Operand, 2-Operand, and 3-Operand Signed IMUL (Slides 48–49 of ch06_part1_2.pdf)
questions.question:
On Slides 48 and 49 (`IMUL`), x86 supports 1-operand, 2-operand, and 3-operand forms of signed multiplication `IMUL`. Trace the three examples:
1) 1-operand (8-bit): `mov al, -10` (`F6h`) / `mov bl, 5` (`05h`) / `imul bl`
2) 2-operand (32-bit): `mov eax, -12` / `mov ebx, 8` / `imul eax, ebx`
3) 3-operand (32-bit): `mov ebx, -12` / `imul eax, ebx, 5`
What are the results and where are they stored?
options: 1) `-10 × 5 = -50 = FFCEh` stored in `AX` (`AH = FFh, AL = CEh`); 2) `-12 × 8 = -96` stored in `EAX`; 3) `-12 × 5 = -60` stored in `EAX` (while `EBX` remains `-12`)
All three forms store their result only in `EDX:EAX`
questions.explanationEn: Slide 48–49 show: (1) 1-operand `imul bl` computes signed `AL × BL = -10 × 5 = -50`. questions.concept: Tracing 8-Bit Signed Overflow on SUB (`-128 - 1`)
questions.question:
Consider the following x86/NASM code or specification:
```nasm
mov al, -128   ; AL = 80h (10000000b)
sub al, 1
```
When `1` is subtracted from `-128` (`80h`) in 8-bit arithmetic, what is the resulting hexadecimal value of `AL`, and what are the values of `CF`, `SF`, `ZF`, and `OF`?
options: AL = 7Fh (+127), CF = 0 (no unsigned borrow since 128 >= 1), SF = 0 (MSB is 0), ZF = 0, and OF = 1 (signed overflow because `-128 - 1 = -129` is outside `[-128, +127]` and wrapped to `+127`!)

questions.question:
Consider the following x86/NASM code or specification:
```nasm
mov ax, -100   ; AX = FF9Ch (-100 signed 16-bit)
mov bl, 7
idiv bl
```
When the 8-bit signed division `idiv bl` divides `AX = -100` by `BL = 7` (`-100 = 7 × (-14) + (-2)`), what are the signed decimal and 8-bit two's complement hexadecimal values of the Quotient `AL` and Remainder `AH`?
questions.explanationEn: In x86 signed division (`IDIV`), the quotient is truncated toward zero (`-100 / 7 = -14 = F2h` in `AL`) and the remainder has the same sign as the dividend (`-100 - 7×(-14) = -2 = FEh` in `AH`), giving `AX = FEF2h`.
